title: What can a quiet conversation do?

The couple Paul calls fellow workers serves through patient instruction. An ordinary conversation becomes part of another person’s fruitful ministry.  When someone needs help understanding Scripture, listen first. Open the passage together. Explain it with care.  You do not need to see the whole future to be faithful in that moment. Careful teaching in a personal conversation Acts 18:24–28 describes Apollos as eloquent, knowledgeable in Scripture and fervent in spirit. Priscilla and Aquila hear him and explain the way of God more accurately. Apollos then helps believers in Achaia and argues from Scripture that Jesus is the Christ. Read alongside their greeting in Romans 16, the encounter shows another aspect of their partnership. Their care serves both Apollos and people he will later teach. We can value a quiet conversation without imagining that Luke has recorded its exact wording or setting. How could you receive correction—or offer it—in a way that helps someone serve Christ? Romans · Chapter 18 — Known by Name Romans sermon 7

title: Who could encourage an apostle?
label: 0:49 film
search_text: Who could encourage an apostle?  In Romans one, Paul longs to visit the believers in Rome and strengthen them.  Then he explains that they will be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith, both theirs and his.  Paul expects to receive encouragement too. The faith of ordinary believers matters even to an apostle.  This helps us see service as something we share. God brings people together who can strengthen one another.  So when you speak with someone at church this week, ask how they are trusting Christ. Listen for what their faith can teach you.  Share honestly too. Faithfulness includes giving encouragement and receiving it. Your place in that conversation matters. Encouragement can travel both ways In Romans 1:11–12, Paul explains his desire to strengthen the church by speaking of encouragement through each other’s faith. His apostolic calling leaves room for receiving encouragement from the people he serves. The book’s opening discussion of Paul’s pastoral posture makes this a practical picture of shared life. A person can have real responsibility and still need the faith, prayers and presence of others. Acknowledging that need gives other members of Christ’s body room to serve. Who encourages you, and do they know what their faith has meant to you? Romans · Chapter 2 — Power to Save Romans sermon 4

title: What is God’s patience inviting us to do?
label: 0:46 film
search_text: What is God’s patience inviting us to do?  In Romans two, Paul challenges the person who judges others while practicing the same things.  Then he asks whether we are taking God’s kindness for granted. His kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.  We can mistake a quiet season for approval, as though nothing going wrong means nothing needs to change.  Paul teaches us to receive patience as an opportunity to turn to God.  So when Scripture exposes a sin you have been excusing, name it honestly before him. Ask for his mercy, and take the next faithful step.  Let kindness lead you to repentance. Patience invites a response Romans 2:1–5 addresses the person who judges others while practicing the same sins. God’s kindness and patience are meant to lead to repentance. Paul warns against mistaking a delayed judgment for permission to remain unchanged. The book’s examination of human accountability brings the hearer into the argument. Recognizing God’s patience can free us to stop comparing ourselves with someone else and acknowledge the mercy we need. What specific response of repentance has God’s patience given you time to make? Romans · Chapter 3 — Without Excuse Romans sermon 11

title: What does adoption add to forgiveness?
label: 0:51 film
search_text: What does adoption add to forgiveness?  Forgiveness answers our guilt. Adoption tells us where we belong.  In Romans eight, Paul says believers have received the Spirit of adoption. By him we cry, Abba, Father.  The Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. Those in Christ belong to God’s family.  Paul also calls them heirs with Christ. That includes suffering with him on the way to glory. Belonging does not mean an easy life.  As you read this passage, notice the family words: Father, children, heirs. Let them shape how you think about your relationship with God.  You are welcomed as his child. Children who can call on their Father Romans 8:12–17 connects life by the Spirit with adoption, prayer and inheritance. Believers are children of God and fellow heirs with Christ. Paul also speaks of suffering with Christ, keeping family belonging and future glory together. The book’s chapter on life in the Spirit draws out this welcome. Forgiveness opens into a relationship in which we can cry to God as Father and depend on his care. Adoption gives the believer a place in a family that includes other children who also need patience and love. How might belonging to God’s family shape the way you pray and receive another believer? Romans · Chapter 8 — Life in the Spirit Romans sermon 26

title: What matters more than winning a food argument?
label: 0:47 film
search_text: What matters more than winning a food argument?  In Romans fourteen, believers disagree about what they can eat. Paul addresses how their freedom affects one another.  Something may be clean in itself, yet another believer may think eating it would be wrong.  If your food grieves that person, Paul says you are no longer walking in love. The person for whom Christ died matters.  This passage concerns disputed practices. It does not make the truth of the gospel optional.  Before insisting on your freedom, ask what will help this brother or sister act in faith. Make room for their conscience.  Pursue peace and build one another up. Freedom carries responsibility for a neighbor Romans 14 addresses disagreements over food and days among people seeking to honor the Lord. Paul tells them to welcome one another and pursue peace and mutual upbuilding. A believer’s freedom must take another believer’s conscience seriously. The book’s chapter on welcoming one another follows Paul’s attention to the person for whom Christ died. This passage calls us to patient care in disputed matters. It should not be used to erase the difference between such disputes and a denial of the gospel itself. What would help a real person grow in faith in the disagreement you are facing? Romans · Chapter 16 — Welcome One Another Romans sermon 52 Romans sermon 53

title: Why did Paul want to preach the gospel to Christians?
label: 0:45 film
search_text: Why did Paul want to preach the gospel to people who already believed?  In Romans one, he thanks God because their faith is known throughout the world. Yet he is eager to preach the gospel to them.  They already belong to Christ, and they still need to hear about him: who he is, how he died and rose, and what God has promised.  The same good news that awakens faith continues to nourish it.  So when a familiar passage comes up, slow down. Ask what it teaches you about Christ.  Christian maturity includes hearing the gospel again, understanding it more deeply, and learning to live from it. The gospel keeps strengthening believers Paul calls the Roman Christians loved by God and called to belong to Christ. He thanks God for their faith, then says he is eager to preach the gospel to them. His eagerness makes sense when we see the gospel as the power of God for salvation and the continuing ground of faith. The opening chapters of Landon’s book trace that connection. Believers keep needing to hear who Jesus is and what God has done through him. Returning to the gospel can deepen assurance, undo boasting and equip us to love the people around us. Which truth about Christ do you need to hear again today? Romans · Chapter 2 — Power to Save Romans sermon 4

title: Why does Paul call grace a gift?
label: 0:47 film
search_text: Why does Paul call grace a gift?  Think about a paycheck. You worked for it, so your employer owes you those wages.  In Romans four, Paul uses that contrast to explain righteousness before God. A wage is earned. A gift is received.  God justifies the ungodly who trust him. Faith receives what God gives through Christ; it does not put God in our debt.  That gift came through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Grace is free to us because Christ paid the cost.  As you read Romans, notice where Paul excludes boasting. Then thank God for the righteousness you could never earn. A gift leaves no room for boasting Romans 3:21–26 locates justification in the redemption accomplished by Jesus Christ. Romans 4 then contrasts a worker’s pay with righteousness counted to the one who trusts God. Paul uses Abraham and David to show that this grace belongs to the story Scripture has been telling all along. Landon’s chapter on justification develops faith as receiving God’s promise. Gratitude and obedience grow from the mercy we have received. They cannot turn that mercy into a debt God owes us. Where are you tempted to measure your welcome with God by what you have earned? Romans · Chapter 4 — Righteous by Faith Romans sermon 15 Romans sermon 16

title: What should a grafted branch remember?
label: 0:51 film
search_text: What should a grafted branch remember?  In Romans eleven, Paul pictures Gentile believers as wild olive branches grafted into an olive tree.  They now share in its nourishing root. But Paul gives them a warning: do not become arrogant toward the other branches.  The branch does not support the root. The root supports the branch.  The picture points to dependence on God’s covenant blessing. Gentile believers have received mercy, and their place gives them no reason to look down on Jewish people.  Paul says they stand through faith.  When you read this passage, let that picture check your pride. Remember the mercy you have received, and respond with humble gratitude. The root supports the branch Romans 11 addresses Gentile believers who have been brought to share in the nourishing root of the olive tree. Paul warns them against boasting over the natural branches and calls them to remember that they stand by faith. Landon’s chapter on mercy develops this into humility and gratitude. Gentile inclusion cannot justify contempt for Jewish people. The image reminds us that we have received a place in a story of promise and mercy that we did not create. Where could gratitude for received mercy replace a sense of superiority? Romans · Chapter 12 — The Depths of Mercy Romans sermon 42

title: Why Romans ends with names
label: 0:49 film
search_text: Why does Romans end with so many names?  After chapters about sin, grace, and life in Christ, Paul greets people. Phoebe had helped many. Prisca and Aquila had risked their lives for him. Mary had worked hard for the church.  Those greetings show us the people living out the gospel. They opened homes, served, and cared for one another. Names matter because people matter.  That makes me pay closer attention to the people around me: the person who encourages me, opens a home, or quietly serves.  As you read Romans sixteen, pause over the names. Then remember someone whose faithfulness has helped you, and thank them. A letter addressed to people Romans ends by naming people whose service took different forms: hospitality, hard work, risk, affection and care. The greetings belong with the letter’s teaching about one body and many members in Romans 12. Paul’s argument has a community in view. Landon’s closing chapter and sermon return to the ordinary settings in which faithfulness grows. A home, a workplace or a conversation can become part of gospel partnership. Paul gives us reason to notice these people without inventing the details of lives he describes only briefly. Whose quiet faithfulness could you thank God for—and acknowledge to them—this week? Romans · Chapter 18 — Known by Name Romans sermon 58

title: When words fail
label: 0:46 film
search_text: Have you ever sat down to pray and had no idea what to say?  Romans eight speaks directly to that weakness. Paul says we do not know what to pray for as we ought. Then he tells us that the Spirit himself intercedes for us.  God knows the mind of the Spirit, whose intercession is according to God's will.  For those who belong to Christ, help is already present in the middle of confusion and grief. You can come to God with the words you have, even when they feel unfinished.  When prayer is difficult today, remember the Spirit's help. Bring your weakness to God, and keep coming. Prayer in the middle of weakness Romans 8 places the Spirit’s help alongside the groaning of creation and the longing of believers for bodily redemption. Difficulty praying belongs within that larger experience of waiting. Paul says the Spirit intercedes according to God’s will. The book’s chapter on life in the Spirit follows this movement from assurance to suffering and prayer. You can bring an unfinished prayer to God while trusting that his care reaches beyond your ability to explain what hurts. Paul’s confidence rests in the Spirit’s help rather than in a particular form of words. What would you bring to God today if you did not have to phrase it perfectly? Romans · Chapter 8 — Life in the Spirit Romans sermon 29

title: What does “good” mean?
label: 0:49 film
search_text: What does Romans eight twenty-eight mean by good?  Paul says that all things work together for good for those who love God and are called according to his purpose.  The next verse names that purpose: being conformed to the image of his Son. God is making his people like Christ.  The surrounding passage speaks honestly about suffering, groaning, and waiting. That gives this promise weight when life is painful and the future is unclear.  We may have to wait without understanding how God is working. But his purpose gives us reason to trust him.  When you return to this familiar promise, read verse twenty-nine with it. Let God's purpose shape your hope. Read the promise with the next verse Romans 8:28 speaks to those who love God and are called according to his purpose. Verse 29 tells us where that purpose leads: conformity to the image of his Son. The surrounding passage includes suffering, waiting and the hope of glory. Landon’s book and sermons read “good” within that whole argument. We should be slow to explain someone’s loss or promise an outcome the passage does not name. Christlikeness and God’s keeping love give the promise its depth even when the present circumstances remain painful. How does verse 29 change what you hear in the promise of verse 28? title: William Tyndale
reference: A lamp, a coat and a Hebrew Bible
label: 1:16 film
search_text: William Tyndale was cold, and his clothes were wearing out. From prison, he asked for a warmer cap, a coat and cloth to mend his leggings. He also asked permission to have a lamp. Long evenings alone in darkness were wearing him down. Above everything else, he wanted a Hebrew Bible, a grammar and a dictionary, so he could keep studying.  Tyndale had helped bring a printed English New Testament into people's hands. Translating depended on friends, printers and people willing to carry the books. Now the man whose work helped others read Scripture needed help himself. His letter ends by entrusting himself to God and the grace of Jesus Christ.  Friends tried to help after his arrest. He was executed the following year. We remember his labor as a servant who trusted in Christ.  Romans says faith comes through hearing the message about Christ. People still need time and practical support to help others hear it.  Is there someone whose service you could strengthen? Ask what would help. A warm meal or a useful book can become part of another person's work for the gospel. A request from prison William Tyndale’s prison letter asks for warmer clothing, a lamp and Hebrew study materials. Its practical details bring a translator’s needs into view: bodily cold, the darkness of the evening and the desire to continue studying Scripture. The surviving text is in Latin. The English version linked below is J. I. Mombert’s nineteenth-century translation, presented with the Latin. Tyndale requests a Hebrew Bible, grammar and dictionary; the letter does not establish that the materials reached him. His work on a printed English New Testament belongs within the longer history of English Bible translation, rather than being the first translation into English of any biblical text. Romans 15:30–33 lets us consider the help and prayer a traveling worker needs. That is a present-day connection to Tyndale’s circumstances, rather than a claim about which passage prompted his request. What practical need might help someone continue work that serves others?

title: Shi Meiyu (Mary Stone)
label: 1:19 film
search_text: A nurse may understand a lesson in training and still need help when a patient is in front of her. Shi Meiyu wanted nurses in China to have words they could use. Known in English as Mary Stone, she translated medical textbooks and training manuals into Chinese.  She'd grown up in a Chinese Christian family and studied medicine in Michigan. Then she returned to China, where caring for patients and teaching nurses became part of her daily work. A clearly explained lesson could help a nurse care for someone Mary would never meet.  The work depended on others, too. Her sister Phoebe, also a doctor, took responsibility for the hospital while Mary continued her studies. Later Mary helped establish the Bethel Mission. War eventually displaced the communities and institutions she helped build.  Romans describes people with different gifts who belong to one body in Christ. God's grace gives us something to offer and people whose help we need.  Perhaps someone could use what you've learned. Take time to explain it in words they can understand. When we teach with patience, we help another person care for a neighbor. That shared work is one way we serve the Lord together. Knowledge that could serve another patient Shi Meiyu, known in English as Mary Stone, studied medicine at the University of Michigan with Kang Cheng and returned to China. Medical care and nursing education developed together in her work. Translating training materials into Chinese helped make knowledge usable by people who would care for patients themselves. Her service depended on colleagues and family. Her sister Phoebe took responsibility for the hospital during further study, and Shi later helped establish the Bethel Mission with Jennie Hughes. War disrupted the communities and institutions in which they worked. Remembering that shared effort gives a fuller account than attributing every hospital or training outcome to one person. The distinction between teaching and direct care can disappear in a useful lesson: what one person learns may become part of another neighbor’s treatment. Romans 12 gives us a way to value these different gifts together. What knowledge could you make more useful to someone else?

title: Rota Waitoa
reference: The pastor who went back to learn
label: 1:23 film
search_text: Rota Waitoa sometimes returned to college after he'd become a pastor. He went back to read, study and spend time with a trusted friend. The responsibilities waiting for him were large, and he needed help with the questions they raised.  Years before his ordination, he'd managed provisions at Saint John's College while studying and teaching younger Maori pupils. In eighteen fifty-three, he became the first Maori ordained in the Anglican Church, after years of training and disagreement over Maori access to ministry.  On the East Coast, a local leader initially opposed his appointment. Later, Waitoa baptized him, and they worked together to build a church.  His later years included the East Coast wars. He opposed the King movement and Pai Marire, and became involved in hostilities.  Romans calls us to sober judgment about ourselves. We belong to one another in Christ, with different gifts received by grace.  Responsibility can make it hard to admit what we need to learn. A return to study, or an honest conversation with someone we trust, can strengthen our service.  What question in your responsibilities needs patient attention? Receive help, and let it become part of the care you offer others. A ministry that still needed learning Rota Waitoa became the first Māori ordained into the Anglican church in 1853 after years of study and service at St John’s College. His East Coast ministry brought responsibilities for which he continued to seek study, friendship and support. G. J. Dempsey’s national biography describes his returns to St John’s to read and renew relationships. It also places his ministry within unequal colonial church structures and records his later involvement in wartime hostilities. Honoring his perseverance does not settle the moral questions surrounding those conflicts or make every missionary assessment of Māori leadership reliable. The return to learning offers a bounded but useful picture: people carrying responsibility still need help. Romans 12 describes a body with differing gifts, and Romans 15 asks the strong to build up their neighbors. Receiving support can become part of what we offer others. Where would returning to study or seeking counsel serve the people who depend on you?

title: Hilary of Poitiers
label: 1:26 film
search_text: Hilary of Poitiers believed that Jesus Christ was truly God before he learned the disputed word bishops used to defend that truth. He explained this while writing from exile.  The churches of the fourth century were divided over how to speak about the Son and the Father. Hilary wanted Christians to confess Christ truthfully. He also knew that hearing an unfamiliar expression didn't always tell you what someone believed.  In his work On the Councils, he explained rival formulas and asked his readers to consider what the words meant. He wanted bishops using different language to recognize where they shared a faithful confession of the Son's divine nature.  That work took patience. He asked for prayer as he offered his writing to fellow Christians.  Romans calls us to welcome one another as Christ has welcomed us, and to glorify God together. We can hold firmly to the truth while taking time to understand another person.  When a Christian's words trouble you, ask what they mean. Give them room to explain. Then speak clearly about what you believe. That kind of attention can help us pursue truth together with love.  Christ has welcomed us by grace. May the way we listen and speak help a brother or sister grow in him. Listening carefully in a doctrinal dispute Hilary of Poitiers wrote On the Councils amid fourth-century disputes over how the church should confess the Son’s relation to the Father. His concern for truth included careful attention to what another person meant by the language being used. In sections 84–92, he considers how terms can be understood or misunderstood and urges patience toward those whose intention may be sound. This is a particular intervention within a serious doctrinal controversy. It should not be turned into a claim that every theological difference is merely verbal. Hilary’s exile belongs to the reign of Constantius II. The later print shown here illustrates how subsequent Christians remembered him; it is neither a contemporary likeness nor proof of the setting it imagines. Romans 12’s call to humility and harmony offers a related challenge to our own speech. What question could help you understand someone’s meaning before answering?

title: Dora Yu
label: 1:19 film
search_text: Dora Yu asked her sister not to write her life story if she died suddenly. She'd read a biography of a friend and thought he would have told parts of it differently. When Dora wrote her own testimony, she wanted people to remember the grace she'd needed.  She was a Chinese Christian teacher, already known for encouraging others. A meeting with an old schoolmate brought back a conflict. Dora remembered losing her temper and wrote that God showed her she needed to confess.  She wanted to wait for the other woman to confess first. She was also concerned about her reputation as a Christian worker. In her own account, she says she obeyed.  Dora could speak about God's love while still needing that love herself. In the preface to her testimony, she pictured meeting her Lord with wonder at his grace.  Romans says Christ died for us while we were still sinners. Those who belong to Christ Jesus face no condemnation. We can face our sin honestly, receive mercy and go on serving.  Perhaps someone helped you follow Jesus by admitting their own need for grace. Let their example encourage you to bring your own failures to Christ. His mercy is our hope. Dora’s own account of grace Dora Yu’s testimony gives us access to how she wanted her Christian service remembered. In its preface she explains her unease with biographies that might tell a person’s life differently from the way the person would tell it. She includes failures as well as mercies for which she gives thanks. Chapter V recalls a conflict with a former schoolmate and Dora’s conviction that she needed to confess her own anger. Concern about her standing as a Christian worker made that obedience difficult. Her account does not supply the other woman’s response or the exact words of the confession. The preface’s exclamation about grace expresses what Dora hoped to say before her Lord; it is not a reported deathbed scene. Her testimony allows us to remember a teacher of the faith as someone who continued to need the Savior’s mercy. How has someone’s honesty about their need for grace helped you follow Christ?

title: Florens Radewijns and the prepared page
reference: The prepared page and the open door
label: 1:25 film
search_text: Before a book could be copied, somebody had to get the pages ready. In medieval Deventer, Florens Radewijns shared that work with the Brethren of the Common Life.  Thomas a Kempis remembered Florens smoothing parchment and ruling lines for the copyists. Florens also helped read and correct the finished books. The household's work helped support its shared life and care for people in need.  People came to the house for counsel, too. Thomas described the interruptions and remembered a phrase Florens used: Once more for the sake of God. He could make room for the visitor or arrange another time.  When we welcome people, we also need wisdom about the responsibilities we've already been given. We can share the work and receive help ourselves.  Romans places our different gifts within one body in Christ. We serve because God has shown us mercy. First Peter calls us to use our gifts with the strength God supplies.  Think of someone whose careful work made your own service possible. Thank that person by name. A prepared room or a thoughtful conversation can become care for someone Christ loves.  His mercy comes before our service. We offer these ordinary acts to him because he's already welcomed us by grace. Making time beside the prepared page Thomas à Kempis’s Life of Florentius describes Florens Radewijns preparing parchment and correcting books, then attending patiently to people who interrupted him. In chapter XIV, paragraph 3, the biography attributes the phrase “Once more for the sake of God” to Florens as he receives another interruption. The attribution comes from this admiring biography, not an autograph quotation or proof that Florens coined the words. J. P. Arthur’s 1905 translation places the passage on printed page 112. Its value lies in the particular remembrance of practical work alongside personal availability. A surviving fifteenth-century copy of a letter attributed to Florens offers a different kind of connection with his written legacy. It is not his handwriting or the page he is said to have prepared in the story. These documents let us encounter both written work and a remembered life of care. When might making room for a person be part of the work God has given you?

title: Mary Magdalene
reference: Called by name and sent with hope
label: 1:25 film
search_text: Mary Magdalene stood outside the tomb, weeping. She'd come while it was still dark and found the stone moved. She told Peter and another disciple that the Lord had been taken away.  Now she looked into the tomb and saw two angels. When they asked why she was crying, she said she didn't know where her Lord had been laid.  She turned and saw Jesus, but didn't recognize him. She thought he was the gardener.  Jesus said, Mary. She recognized her teacher. The Lord she was seeking was alive. He gave her a message for his brothers, and she went to the disciples with the news that she'd seen him.  Luke also tells us Mary had received healing and helped support Jesus' ministry. The woman who needed care had become someone with good news to carry.  Romans directs our hope to Christ who died and rose again, and whose love holds us through suffering.  If grief has left you struggling to find words, Mary's story can help you look toward Christ. Her tears were real when Jesus met her. The risen Lord gave her hope through his own presence and his word.  Our Savior is alive. His mission includes people who have wept. May his resurrection give you courage to encourage someone else with the hope he's given you. The risen Jesus calls Mary by name John 20:1–18 follows Mary Magdalene from the discovery of the open tomb through her grief to her encounter with the risen Jesus. She recognizes him when he addresses her by name, and she carries his message to the disciples. The announcement grows out of a personal encounter with the living Lord. John’s account does not identify Mary with other women who share her name. The scene is enough to see her grief, recognition and witness without combining distinct biographies. Later Christian art bears witness to the church’s long reflection on this encounter. Such images can enrich that history of reception while remaining distinct from evidence about Mary’s appearance or the physical arrangement of the garden. Who has helped you hear the good news as a personal word of hope?

title: Althea Brown Edmiston
reference: Learning from the people you serve
label: 1:34 film
search_text: Althea Brown Edmiston went to the Congo as a teacher. An African American Christian, she arrived in nineteen oh two and taught at a girls' home before working among the Bushoong people.  Learning their language became part of her service. She compiled a grammar and dictionary and helped provide reading materials. These were tools for understanding and using a language the people already spoke.  That work required sustained attention to other people's words. A teacher arriving in a community also had things to learn.  The work belonged to a wider circle. Althea's husband, Alonzo, served in education and agriculture. Congolese Christians taught, printed and carried the work forward. Their labor helped people hear and learn, too.  Romans asks how people will hear the good news of Christ. Around that hearing there can be years of patient preparation, and people whose contributions are easy to overlook.  God has given his people different gifts for one another. A carefully prepared book can help a reader you may never meet. Time spent understanding another person's words can help you speak to them with greater care.  Who helped make something understandable for you? Thank them for the attention they gave. As you serve, take time to learn from the people you hope to help. Christ's grace frees us to receive as well as give. Language work within a larger community Althea Brown Edmiston, an African American educator, arrived in the Congo in 1902. Teaching, learning the local language and preparing useful reading tools belonged together in her work among the Bushoong people. Presbyterian Historical Society descriptions of the Edmiston papers preserve evidence of educational, linguistic and mission work. Her grammar and dictionary are identified in that record; a bibliographic listing is not the same as having read the whole grammar. Her husband Alonzo and Congolese teachers, printers and Christians also contributed to the larger work. The language already belonged to its speakers. A foreign worker’s task required learning from them, and their contributions should remain visible alongside the papers preserved under the missionaries’ names. Romans 12 helps us consider the many gifts and patient preparations that make learning possible. Whose patient preparation helped make something understandable to you?

title: Nerses and Armenian communities of care
reference: A place at the shared table
label: 1:29 film
search_text: Nerses, a church leader in fourth-century Armenia, shared his table with people who were often pushed aside.  The Armenian history attributed to Pawstos describes him dividing food with his own hands and tending to wounded people. Blind, deaf and disabled guests sat among his companions.  Care also became a shared responsibility. Bishops gathered at Ashtishat to arrange provision for people in need. There were houses for the sick and destitute, and support for widows and orphans.  Those arrangements expected recipients to remain in designated places instead of going out to beg. Shelter came with restrictions on the people receiving it.  Romans calls believers to contribute to one another's needs and pursue hospitality. We do this because God has already shown us mercy in Christ. Our generosity can't purchase his love.  A church needs organized provision and people willing to keep promises. It also needs the kindness of shared company. As we offer help, we can listen to the person receiving it and respect their choices.  Who could you welcome to a meal or a conversation? Ask what would help, and listen to the answer. Give someone room to be known as a person whose company you value, with a place in your shared life. A table and organized care in Armenia P’awstos’s History of the Armenians remembers fourth-century bishop Nerses sharing food with poor and disabled people and tending wounds himself. Book IV, chapter 4 also describes organized provision for sick people, widows and orphans. This is a later literary account of the fourth-century church, not a contemporary hospital ledger. It brings together charitable institutions, episcopal ideals and religious expectations. The arrangements it describes could provide shelter while restricting recipients’ freedom to leave designated places. Compassion must attend to dignity and agency as well as material provision. The table gives us a personal question alongside the institutional one: who is welcome to share ordinary life with us? Romans 12’s instructions about generosity and hospitality invite both practical organization and relationships in which people can belong. Where could practical help also make room for friendship and another person’s agency?

title: Peter
reference: Mercy for the one who would strengthen others
label: 1:28 film
search_text: Before Peter denied knowing Jesus, Jesus spoke about the brothers Peter would one day strengthen.  Peter was sure he was ready for prison and death. That night, beside a courtyard fire, he denied knowing his Lord. When the rooster crowed, he went out weeping.  After the resurrection, Jesus met him beside the sea. There was breakfast waiting. Then Jesus asked Peter about his love and entrusted him with care for his sheep.  The servant who would feed others had needed mercy himself.  At Pentecost, Peter stood with the eleven and proclaimed Jesus as Lord and Christ. His failure hadn't erased Christ's call.  He still needed correction. Later, Paul opposed him publicly for withdrawing from Gentile believers. Those neighbors mattered, and Peter's conduct had hurt their fellowship.  Romans says we're justified by God's grace as a gift. That grace gives us courage to face what we've done and receive honest help. Consequences and questions about responsibility still deserve care.  Perhaps shame has made you afraid to come near Jesus. Tell him the truth. Ask a trustworthy believer to walk with you as you repent and make amends where you can. The Savior who knew Peter's failure also knew how to call him toward faithful love. Restoration leads toward care for others Luke 22 records Jesus’s warning that Peter will deny him and his promise of prayer for Peter. The instruction looks beyond failure toward strengthening his brothers. John 21 later places a renewed call to follow Jesus alongside the charge to care for his sheep. The denial remains part of Peter’s story, and so does Christ’s restoring care. Scripture gives us a redemptive arc rather than requiring us to construct one from uncertain reports. We can see that Peter’s future service depends on the Lord who knows him fully. The stained-glass image shown below belongs to a much later Christian setting and depicts the giving of keys. It illustrates the history of Peter’s remembrance, not the lakeside conversation in John 21. How might receiving Christ’s mercy prepare you to care more patiently for someone else?

title: Christiana Tsai, Mary Leaman and their friends
reference: A place in Christ’s shared life
label: 1:25 film
search_text: Christiana Tsai had traveled widely to speak about Jesus. Later, illness confined much of her life to a darkened room. Light hurt her eyes, and faith didn't make that pain disappear.  Her friend Mary Leaman stayed part of her life through illness, war and displacement. They had served in China and eventually settled in Pennsylvania. People still came to visit Christiana, receive encouragement and talk about serving Christ.  In nineteen fifty-six, Moses Chow and Ted and Leona Choy met with her in Paradise. They shared a concern for Chinese students. Bible studies and publishing grew, and Ambassadors for Christ was founded several years later.  Christiana and Mary gave part of their property to the ministry. In time, its headquarters moved there. Friends and their shared gifts helped a woman living with severe limits take part in work reaching far beyond her room.  Romans tells Christ's people to welcome one another and share their gifts as members of one body. Illness doesn't cancel that belonging.  Perhaps your strength has changed. You still have a place among people who love you. And if a friend has become harder to visit, make time. Listen to what they have to share. Let them receive your care and offer their own. Friendship and ministry within physical limits Christiana Tsai’s sensitivity to light confined much of her life to a darkened room. Her friendship with Mary Leaman continued through changing circumstances, and people still sought her encouragement. This limitation should not be relabeled blindness or treated as something faith required her to overcome. Ambassadors for Christ’s institutional history records a meeting with Tsai in 1956, the organization’s founding in 1963, a shared property gift in 1966 and the later headquarters move in 1974. Those are distinct events. Moses Chow, Ted and Leona Choy, Leaman and other workers belong within the account. The value of Tsai’s life cannot be measured by an organization’s later size. Her relationships give a particular picture of fellowship continuing within illness, with help both received and offered. How could your church include someone whose strength or mobility has changed?

title: Elida García de Falcón and Clotilde Falcón Náñez
reference: The hands behind the finished page
label: 1:30 film
search_text: Elida García de Falcón wrote the Spanish translations by hand. Her daughter Clotilde typed the pages.  Their shared work helped Spanish-speaking Methodist women use material prepared for the church's service. Elida brought gifts developed through teaching, poetry and newspaper writing in Texas. Clotilde helped those words become pages other women could use.  When illness interrupted her mother's work, Clotilde continued. Together, their contribution extended across twenty-six years.  Elida also translated hymns. Choosing words carefully could help a neighbor take part in worship and understand a task the church was doing together.  Her pastor remembered a home where people came for counsel, and where sick or needy neighbors found shelter. The woman working over a page also made room for people at her door.  Romans describes Christ's people as one body with different gifts. Each belongs through grace, and each has something to offer. A finished translation carried the labor of a mother and daughter, including work readers might never notice.  Who helps your gifts reach someone else? Think of the person who prepares a room, checks your words or carries on when your strength gives out. Thank them for what they actually do. You may have a part in helping their gifts reach others, too. The handwriting and the typing both mattered Elida García de Falcón translated program materials into Spanish by hand; her daughter Clotilde Falcón Náñez typed them. When illness interrupted Elida’s work, Clotilde continued. Their shared work helped Spanish-speaking Methodist women take part in the church’s service. The biography records Elida’s program-book work from 1943 to 1964 and describes the combined translation effort across twenty-six years. Those are different spans, not a basis for inventing an exact final date. Her teaching, poetry, journalism and hymn translation form part of the wider background. Remembering both women helps us see how a finished page can carry several people’s gifts. Translation, preparation and continuation each made the material usable. Romans 12 gives such shared service a place within the life of one body. Who helps your work reach others, and how could you acknowledge their contribution?

title: Michael Sattler
reference: The love he asked them to keep
label: 1:07 film
search_text: Michael Sattler wrote to a church he couldn't visit. He was in prison, and the people at Horb were still on his mind.  In his letter, he urged them to love patiently, help those in need, and care for weaker members. He asked them to remember the prisoners in prayer.  His concern reached into his own household. If he died, he wanted the church to care for his wife. He placed that need before people he loved, while the outcome was still uncertain.  He also wished he could keep working. Yet he trusted that the Lord could raise up another worker.  The letter lets us see a servant of Christ who needed the very care he urged others to give. The fellowship he described included people receiving help as well as offering it.  When someone you love can no longer do what they once did, keep making room for them. Pray with them. Ask what would help. Our fellowship in Christ includes the days when we need others to carry more of the work. A letter about love from confinement In a letter to the congregation at Horb, Michael Sattler calls the believers to love and makes a practical request concerning care for his wife. The counsel belongs to the period of his confinement before his execution in 1527. His wife Margaretha was also executed shortly afterward. The letter’s concern for community and household care gives us more to remember than the manner of his death. An early printed volume dated 1527 preserves both the Schleitheim confession and the Horb letter. They are distinct texts within the same surviving volume; neither should be shown as an autograph. Romans 12 helps us reflect on love that takes concrete responsibility under pressure. Honoring Sattler’s witness does not require treating every theological position associated with him as the shared confession of all Christians. Who might need practical care while someone they depend on is absent or in danger?

title: Satoko Kitahara
reference: She joined them in the work
label: 1:12 film
search_text: In postwar Tokyo, families at Arinomachi made a living collecting and selling discarded materials. Satoko Kitahara came to share their work.  She had become a Christian, and her faith drew her toward neighbors living with the losses of war. She helped children and joined the scrap collecting that supported the community.  Her service took place beside people who were already working for their families and their future. Their lives involved cooperation, skill and decisions of their own.  Tuberculosis brought periods when Satoko needed rest. Illness changed what she could do, while her connection with Arinomachi continued.  When the community faced relocation, the needed funds were eventually gathered. That achievement belonged to a shared effort, not to one person alone.  Her story gives us a question to carry into our own service. Have we taken time to know the people we hope to help?  Ask about the work already being done. Listen to what your neighbors need and what they can teach you. Love can grow as we learn to work together. Shared work in postwar Tokyo Satoko Kitahara came to know the families of Arinomachi through the Franciscan brother Zeno. She helped children learn and joined the collection of scrap on which the community’s livelihood depended. These families were neighbors with skills and agency, not merely recipients of an outsider’s generosity. The Catholic biographical summary describes her Christian conversion in 1949, her illness and the effort to obtain land when the community faced relocation. Many people contributed to the fundraising. Her tuberculosis should not be attributed to a specific cause without evidence, and her faithfulness should not be made into a promise of recovery. The story invites attention to the difference between helping at a distance and learning to share life. Her contribution mattered within the work of a larger community. What could you learn by sharing a task with people you usually think of only as needing help?

title: Eadburga
label: 1:11 film
search_text: A missionary's letters preserve the name of a woman whose help had reached him more than once. Her name was Eadburga.  Boniface thanked this abbess for books and garments that had comforted him in distress. The gratitude was personal. He remembered what her kindness had meant to him.  He also asked for a copy of Peter's letters written in gold. He wanted the people hearing him preach to see the honor given to Scripture. The request survives; it doesn't tell us that the book was completed.  Eadburga's repeated help gave Boniface reason to thank God. He could ask for what he needed because he had already known her kindness.  Mission depended on people who received support as well as those who supplied it. Books and practical provision could strengthen someone serving far away.  Is there a worker you could ask about an actual need? A thoughtful question may reveal something a general offer misses.  And if someone has helped you keep going, tell them what their kindness meant. A letter of thanks can honor work that others never see. The books that supported a journey Boniface’s letters thank Eadburga for books and church garments that had encouraged him in his work. Another letter asks for the letters of Peter to be copied in gold. The request reveals how a preacher serving far from home depended on other people’s resources and skill. Edward Kylie’s 1911 translation prints these exchanges as letters XIV and XV; the corresponding Tangl numbers are 35 and 30. The gold manuscript is a requested commission, not a documented completed gift. The letters also do not establish that Eadburga personally copied every page. Her precise identification with later accounts of particular abbesses remains debated. The attested exchange is enough to preserve a woman’s name within the practical support of mission. Romans 15 likewise allows us to see prayer and material help as participation in the work. What resource or practical provision would genuinely help a worker you know?

title: Who holds the world together?
label: 0:42 film
search_text: When life feels uncertain, it's easy to live as though everything depends on you. God asked Job where he was when the earth's foundations were laid. Job was suffering, and God's questions drew his attention to wisdom and power far beyond his own.  Job came to confess how little he understood. Hebrews tells us that Jesus upholds all things by his powerful word. You can bring your unanswered questions to him today.  Care for the people he's placed near you, and ask for help with what you can't carry. Your Savior is holding more than you can see. The Creator answers Job Job 38 brings God’s questions into a story of profound suffering. Foundations, sea and dawn expose the limits of Job’s knowledge. The passage does not give him a complete explanation of every loss; it brings him before the Creator whose understanding exceeds his own. Hebrews 1:1–4 explicitly identifies the Son as the one through whom God made the world and who sustains it. Reading these passages together offers Christians a reason for humility and trust without suggesting that unanswered questions are trivial. Landon’s discussion of creating and sustaining power supplies the Romans connection. Where might you need trust and patient companionship while an explanation remains beyond reach? Romans · Chapter 2 — Power to Save Romans · Chapter 3 — Without Excuse Romans sermon 6

title: Keep sowing without knowing
label: 0:41 film
search_text: You can do faithful work without knowing how it will turn out. Ecclesiastes pictures a person sowing seed in the morning and continuing their work in the evening. The writer says we don't know which effort will prosper.  He also reminds us how much we don't understand about God's work. That gives us a humble way to face tomorrow. Plant the seed that's yours to plant: encourage a friend, teach a child, keep a promise.  Ask God for wisdom, do your work with care, and leave room for an outcome you can't yet see. Faithful work without control of the harvest Ecclesiastes 11:4–6 observes that waiting for ideal conditions can prevent the work of sowing. Human beings do not fully know God’s work or which effort will prosper. The instruction is to continue working within that uncertainty. The agricultural language invites reflection on ordinary responsibilities, but it does not guarantee success for every project. Helping a neighbor or teaching patiently can be faithful even when we cannot predict the result. This is an additional biblical connection with the book’s account of dependence on the Creator; it is not a claim that the Romans sermon expounded Ecclesiastes. What worthwhile task could you continue without demanding certainty about its outcome? Romans · Chapter 2 — Power to Save Romans · Chapter 3 — Without Excuse Romans sermon 6

title: What worry can’t give you
label: 0:38 film
search_text: Worry can fill a day without adding a single hour to your life. Jesus points his hearers toward birds that are fed and flowers that are clothed. Then he reminds them that their heavenly Father knows what they need.  He calls them to seek God's kingdom, and reminds them that each day has troubles of its own. You can bring your anxious thoughts to the Father and ask for help with the next step. Name one concern in prayer.  Then consider one faithful thing you can do today, trusting the Father who already knows your needs. Birds, flowers and the Father’s knowledge Matthew 6:25–34 asks anxious disciples to consider birds and flowers within Jesus’s teaching about their heavenly Father. The invitation moves toward seeking God’s kingdom and facing the trouble of the present day. Jesus acknowledges that the day has trouble. A beautiful field is therefore no promise that distress will instantly disappear. The passage directs attention toward the Father who knows his children’s needs. Its reassurance comes from Jesus’s teaching, rather than from scenery alone, and can accompany patient care for someone whose anxiety persists. What would seeking God’s kingdom look like within the responsibilities of today? Romans · Chapter 2 — Power to Save Romans · Chapter 3 — Without Excuse Romans sermon 6

title: Your next breath
label: 0:40 film
search_text: Your next breath is easy to overlook. We make plans for our day while life itself keeps arriving as a gift. In Acts seventeen, Paul tells the people of Athens that God made the world and gives everyone life and breath.  Before your day's work even begins, you've already received something you couldn't give yourself. Let that ordinary gift lead you to thank him. You can begin with a simple prayer: Father, thank you for giving me life today.  Help me use it to love you and serve someone near me. Life received from the Maker In Acts 17:22–31, Paul speaks to people in Athens about the God who made the world and gives life and breath. He challenges the idea that God depends on human provision or can be represented by an object people make. The address moves from creation and dependence to seeking God, repentance, judgment and the resurrection of Jesus. A moment of gratitude for breath belongs within that larger summons. Romans 1:20–21 also connects creation’s testimony with the response of honor and thanksgiving. Nature’s witness points toward the Creator; the good news of Christ must still be told. How could gratitude for life become a response to the God who gives it? Romans · Chapter 2 — Power to Save Romans · Chapter 3 — Without Excuse Romans sermon 6

title: The God who names the stars
label: 0:40 film
search_text: Do you ever feel too small to be noticed? Isaiah forty invites us to look at the stars. Their Creator calls them all by name.  Then Isaiah speaks to people who feel that God has overlooked them. The Maker of the whole earth never grows weary, and he gives strength to the weary. You can bring him the tiredness you've been carrying.  Waiting for the Lord may still mean taking one slow step through a difficult day. When you look up tonight, remember who made those stars, and ask him for strength to take your next step. The stars and a weary people Isaiah 40:26–31 addresses Jacob and Israel’s fear that their way is hidden from God. The prophet directs them to the Creator who calls the stars by name, then speaks of the strength he gives to the weary. The scale of the heavens serves a deeply personal reassurance. The Christian application should preserve that original setting rather than erase it. Waiting on the Lord is not a technique for instant physical recovery. The passage gives tired people reason to depend on the God whose power and understanding exceed their own. The sky directs attention to him; Isaiah’s words explain the promise. Where do you need to hear that weariness has not made you invisible to God? Romans · Chapter 2 — Power to Save Romans · Chapter 3 — Without Excuse Romans sermon 6

title: A sea full of wisdom
label: 0:44 film
search_text: The sea can look empty from the shore. Beneath the surface, life fills places we rarely see. The psalmist praises God for the many things he's made, and says he made them in wisdom.  He points us toward the sea, filled with creatures both small and great. The world holds more of God's work than any of us can take in. You don't have to understand every creature to begin praising its Maker.  Next time you notice something living, slow down long enough to look closely. Let your wonder become worship: Lord, how wise you are in all you've made. A living world dependent on God Psalm 104:24–30 praises the wisdom of God’s many works, then draws attention to the wide sea and its creatures. The psalm moves from delight in their variety to their dependence on God for food and breath. This is worshipful poetry, rather than a catalogue of species or a scientific count. Its language about Leviathan should not be made into an unsupported identification of a modern animal. A closer look at the sea can become an occasion for thanksgiving while the psalm teaches us whom to thank. The creatures share our dependence on their Maker. What part of creation could you notice carefully enough to thank God for it specifically? Romans · Chapter 2 — Power to Save Romans · Chapter 3 — Without Excuse Romans sermon 6
